Recent breakthroughs using network controllability revealed how individual brain regions can affect the whole brain, guided by the brain's structural framework.
Yet, controlling entire brain activity might be impractical, and it is not always necessary.
A more crucial inquiry is whether individual brain areas can regulate specific target subsystems, although this area of research remains poorly understood.

A closer examination was conducted on the role of non-locality in determining motion, the interplay between kernel structure and material non-penetration, as well as the influence of PD kernel non-linearity on predicting fracture development. Finally, an exploration is initiated on adapting BB-PD to model fluids within the context of fading memory materials, suggesting directions for enhanced understanding of fluid dynamics through peridynamics. This review aims to promote a more in-depth discussion on the underlying aspects of bond-based peridynamics and their applications. This work has been influenced by the discussions and collaborations with numerous colleagues and is meant to contribute positively to the PD research community. Rather than aiming to provide an exhaustive historical account of the PD development, the primary objective is to stimulate reflections on the theory and its numerical representations, as well as the opportunities and challenges that they present. It employs ensemble distillation and transfers model outputs as soft labels to participating clients and a central server via a public data set. Unlike conventional Federated Learning, such as Federated Averaging, which increases communication complexity with model size, Federated Distillation reduces communication complexity by utilizing the size of the distillation data set. We analyzed the effects of varying distillation data sets on communication efficiency and performance under three scenarios: when clients and the server have different models, when clients have multiple models, and when the server's model evolves over time. Our findings indicate that selecting a suitable distillation data set is crucial to achieving both efficient communication and optimal performance, as it affects both the amount of data exchanged and the final model quality. Furthermore, the choice of distillation data set influences the ability of Federated Distillation to handle scenarios not encountered during training, as it affects the soft labels sent to participants. We also compared the communication efficiency of Federated Distillation to that of Federated Averaging, as well as to a more recent QD-Learning method, which uses quantized data exchange. As a result, Federated Distillation offers better communication efficiency for larger models, although Averaging may be more suitable for small models and data sets. Additionally, the Distillation paradigm can be combined with QD-Learning to achieve a balance between communication efficiency and model quality

The primary mechanisms driving these emissions involve the rapid ionization of chromospheric layers and radiative energy transfer from the chromosphere to lower atmospheric layers, a phenomenon known as back-warming. This paper focuses on distinguishing between these two processes as the source of the enhanced Balmer continuum observed in a flare event. To accomplish this, we employed the integration of observational data from the IRIS and FERMI Gamma Burst Monitor during a mini flare event. The results of our analysis reveal a temporal coincidence between the Balmer continuum excess and the HXR emission. Moreover, the shape of the 2832 SJIs brightness peak, primarily resulting from the Balmer continuum excess, mirrors the FERMI/GBM light curve. The electron-beam flux detected by FERMI/GBM corresponds to the flux required in radiative transfer models to produce the observed Balmer continuum excess. medical image segmentation has achieved great success with deep learning models built around convolutional operations. Convolutional neural networks benefit from desirable characteristics like sparse connections, weight sharing, and translation symmetry. In contrast, our work presents a novel approach relying solely on self-attention mechanisms between adjacent image patches, bypassing convolutional operations entirely. For a 3D image block, our network partitions it into a specified number of smaller patches, calculates a one-dimensional representation for each patch, and predicts the central patch's segmentation based on the patch embeddings' self-attention interactions. Notably, our proposed model outperforms current state-of-the-art convolutional neural networks on three datasets. Additionally, we develop strategies for pre-training this model on vast unlabeled image collections. Our experiments indicate that with pre-training, the advantages can be significant, and the benefits can extend to multiple related segmentation tasks. Our source code is available at https://github.com/fatesary/AttentionBasedSegmentation.

This problem involves numerous nodes connected to a central node, exchanging concise messages, 
each holding noisy samples from the same regression equation. 
The central node needs to accurately find and replicate the regression vector's support, 
under strict computation and communication limits.

the vector's support, at a communication cost linearly scalable. 
Our simulated data also demonstrates how these distributed OMP-based algorithms match the performance of 
more sophisticated methods in many instances, even outperforming them at times, 
while requiring significantly less communication to operate. 
Our tested data further indicates that the spread of data across multiple nodes affects how well these algorithms work. 
Overall, our research shows that these distributed algorithms are capable of exact support recovery

Through extended interactions, agents can develop awareness about their teammates to counteract the limitations imposed by partial observability, but existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods rarely exploit local information for this purpose. To tackle this challenge, a novel approach called multi-agent Local Information Decomposition for Awareness of teammates (LINDA) is presented, which enables agents to decompose and learn from local information to create awareness about their team members. LINDA models this awareness as probabilistic variables and employs representation learning to maximize the awareness' relevance to teammates' actual behavior, measured through mutual information. LINDA is flexible and can be easily integrated with various existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods. Experimental results demonstrate that LINDA successfully extracts meaningful awareness from limited local observations, ultimately improving collaborative performance and achieving better outcomes, particularly in complex tasks. A similar approach called LINDA-HC is also developed, which utilizes historical data to create awareness, revealing its potential for applications in settings with limited current local observations. Model uncertainty, also referred to as epistemic uncertainty, is a concept that measures a model's expected prediction error beyond random noise. In this paper, a novel metric called pathwise epistemic uncertainty for estimating Q-value functions is introduced, accompanied by a method for approximating its upper limit known as the F-value. Experimental testing with Deep Q-Networks reveals that measuring uncertainty in reinforcement learning can serve as a reliable indicator of training progress. Building upon this discovery, a novel approach is proposed, Critic Confidence Guided Exploration (CCGE), where an actor-critic algorithm incorporates guidance from an existing oracle policy when the learner is uncertain, minimizing the impact of unnecessary random actions during training. Implementing CCGE on Soft Actor-Critic using the F-value upper bound metric in popular Gym environments resulted in improved sample efficiency and higher episodic rewards compared to the vanilla Soft Actor-Critic algorithm. The influence of CCGE on policies' behavior and their potential applications is discussed in the final section. The research presented here is openly sourced at https://github.com/jamiejp1/CCGE. As a result, it has become crucial to effectively maintain these shared files, especially in keeping them updated to the most recent version of the reused code. This study employs a complex network approach to investigate the file maintenance practices of authors who contribute to multiple repositories, including those involving clone-and-own or forking scenarios. Our analysis centers around two key concepts: (a) the level of updating performed on shared files, taking into account their repository chain length; and (b) the distribution of updated files within these chains. Kalman-Bucy initially illustrated that minimum variance estimation has a duality link to a linear quadratic optimal control problem, which also provides a concrete method for deriving the Kalman filter from the optimal control solution. Building upon Kalman-Bucy's findings, this work expands on this relationship by generalizing it to nonlinear systems, specifically those governed by continuous-time Markov processes with nonlinear, noise-affected observations. Furthermore, this work addresses criticisms leveled at Kalman-Bucy's initial proof by Aoki and Yavin, which argued for Kalman-Bucy's conclusion based on a weaker set of premises. In contrast, this work presents an alternative proof that is grounded in a specific model structure, which specifically excludes the use of the "posterior i independence" assumption. As such, this representation offers a more accurate representation of the nonlinear filter equation, which in turn provides a more transparent explanation for its key computational aspects. Our study investigates whether the recent surge in DNN capabilities has led to improved insights into human visual processing during object recognition. By examining how both humans and DNNs locate and utilize essential visual cues when categorizing everyday objects, we reveal a concerning paradox: the higher the DNN's accuracy in object classification, the less aligned it becomes with the visual strategies used by humans. Capturing the cerebellar cortex's tightly foliated appearance is challenging due to its convoluted surface and the time-consuming process of manual segmentation. While human experts can contribute to segmentation quality, current automated labeling methods are limited by their susceptibility to errors. A new, 20 micrometer resolution dataset offers an enhanced platform for semantic segmentation compared to 1mm resolution magnetic resonance imaging. To bypass manual annotation requirements, we suggest training a model to automatically transfer annotated data from the Allen Brain Human Brain Atlas to the BigBrain dataset without supervision, accounting for staining and spacing variations. However, discrepancies in staining between the datasets hinder previous attempts to create meaningful segmentation masks, and histological preparations pose an additional challenge. To address these issues, our two-stage approach first aligns the Allen Brain cerebellum with the BigBrain's spatial layout, and then employs a self-training strategy incorporating a confidence map to guide the model's learning from noisy pseudo-labels iteratively. This method has proven effective in qualitative tests and demonstrated a 2.6% loss reduction over alternative approaches. Furthermore, our solution has potential applications in visualizing the cerebellar cortex and understanding its role in disease, as well as contributing to the development of more accurate brain mapping techniques. The proposed system, along with the associated code, has been successfully integrated into the OpenBigBrain platform and is available at: https://openbigbrain.net/.

An essential component for constructing large-scale integrated quantum networks is an integrated quantum memory for polarization qubits. However, the emerging need for privacy protection techniques in smart contracts remains inadequately addressed. Specifically, the feasibility of securely implementing Multi-party Computation (MPC) in smart contracts remains understudied, particularly with respect to the trade-offs of cost, flexibility, and security. This paper proposes TENET, a modular and adaptable framework for confidential smart contracts that leverages a trusted execution environment (TEE) network to address the challenges of supporting MPC-enabled contracts in a secure and efficient manner. Key features of TENET include anonymous MPC negotiation, atomic and fair output distribution, and constant transaction overhead. Our results show that TENET can achieve MPC security with only three transactions and outperform state-of-the-art solutions in both theoretical and practical evaluations, involving scenarios with two to eleven parties, at a cost that is 0.55 to 0.98 times the baseline (with an average of 0.91 times the baseline). Additionally, TENET has been implemented in actual Ethereum smart contracts. Further details are available at https://tenet-confidential-blockchain.github.io

To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. Extending the time for treatment is considered an effective strategy for improving admissions; nonetheless, empirical evidence supporting this claim is difficult to gather. context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic challenges in inverse computation, while the other, known as the inverse homomorphism attack, allows an adversary to obtain sensitive data of users by exploiting code inversion. The results from our experiments on four diverse datasets clearly show that both attacks are successful and can retrieve users' sensitive data particularly when poisoning instances are chosen carefully. This highlights the necessity for developers to adopt more efficient user codings to prevent such attacks and ensure secure computing in practice. The proposed attacks as well as the code used for this study are both available online for the benefit of the scientific community. The research we conducted here aims to illustrate the vulnerability of actual VFL implementations to data poisoning attacks. Therefore, we suggest adopting several effective strategies that can enhance the security of users' data in particular, and federated learning in general. A detailed examination further distinguishes $M^*$ from M by identifying a specific, invariant characteristic that is present in the former but absent in the latter. Our work also shows that none of the known M-class hypersurfaces feature this distinctive characteristic. Our findings can be summarised by saying that a compact, orientable hypersurface is conformally flat if and only if it is either a torus or belongs to the $M^*$ class. Our research further reveals that non-compact hypersurfaces can be part of the M class. Specifically, we establish that the set of all conformally flat hypersurfaces is either empty or consists of exactly one surface, a torus, or an infinite number of connections. Our study follows recent research by Calabi, Ebin, and others, and our analysis focuses particularly on the relationship between two key energy functionals, $E$ and $\tilde{E}$.

The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Moreover, it employs a novel loss function that distinguishes between pseudo-labels and true labels to prevent the distortion of node representations. Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. Interestingly, this distribution has heavy tails, meaning that most nodes remove few neighbors, but a small fraction of nodes remove a significantly large number of nodes, similar to the effects observed in scale-free networks. training machine learning models can be a daunting task, and often impossible to achieve, so transfer learning becomes a feasible solution. Transfer learning allows for utilizing pre-trained models on new, unrelated tasks by leveraging the knowledge acquired from previous training. However, determining which model to use or how to modify them is extremely challenging, as many transfer learning methods have numerous, uncharted pathways. A novel method called HOP introduces an efficient search technique to navigate the graph of possible models, guiding the search towards those with greater potential for success. By utilizing meta-learning information, such as loss curves and model gradients, HOP can predict the effectiveness of potential models on unseen tasks, outperforming common heuristic approaches. Furthermore, HOP incorporates an innovative technique to detect when tasks share common underlying concepts, resulting in enhanced performance when enabled. In extensive experiments, HOP demonstrated the ability to find better models than current state-of-the-art systems, particularly when tasked with identifying task-agnostic models. HOP's code and supporting data are available online. The ability of HOP to find and optimize models based on underlying task concepts holds significant potential for numerous areas, such as cross-domain and cross-task research, and may be expanded upon in future work. By fine-tuning these concepts, researchers can develop a more effective system for finding the best models, resulting in improved performance and increased understanding of the underlying task

These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and, in doing so, trigger a significant discrepancy in pressure readings. Our research shows that the malfunctions induced by this technique can fool the building management system, potentially allowing pathogens to escape from NPRs. Our study offers several measures that could mitigate this threat, including conducting regular maintenance to identify vulnerable sensors, implementing noise-filtering systems, or redesigning DPSs with higher fundamental frequencies. Our research also suggests that we can use machine learning algorithms, such as deep learning, to improve pressure estimation and protect against potential attacks. Our study also offers several protocols that facility administrators can use to test their systems for vulnerability and provides guidelines for mitigating the risks. Furthermore, we have developed a prototype system called SoundWave that uses machine learning to protect NPRs from malicious audio

Our research focuses on a new approach for modeling a complex data distribution when the training data is distributed unevenly across multiple clients and cannot be shared. Our objective is to create a centralized representation of the distribution without exposing the individual client data, and using common image benchmarks, we found existing solutions fail in this context due to client drift. It achieves this through extensive local training, improving upon prior work with substantial gains, and we also initiate a new discussion on optimizing FEDGAN with adaptive local steps. Our results show EFFGAN efficiently learns a precise and diverse data representation compared to the current state-of-the-art, and it achieves this with significantly fewer local updates than traditional federated averaging, highlighting its potential for reducing latency and improving user experience. , researchers at Li et al. predicted and proved, through experimentation, that a stationary heat profile can emerge in a system where heat is supposed to be diffusing - effectively indicating heat "freezes" its movement. This phenomenon has analogies with the framework of wave physics where stationary and moving patterns can represent parity-time APT symmetry and its breakdown. Their experiment consisted of two rings with opposite rotational directions that interact thermally. At a particular rotation speed - known as an exceptional point, where symmetry breaks - heat transitions between moving and stationary states. Notably, this peculiar behavior can be accurately explained using traditional heat transfer methods incorporating analysis for similarity and scaling. In our work, we demonstrate that the system can be categorized into distinct regions based on widely-used dimensionless parameters presented in a regime map. Furthermore, this exceptional point sits at the boundary between these regions, marking a balance between thermal connection and mechanical activity. In this investigation, two strategies for creating the most efficient engines are considered, specifically (1) using hybrid quantum systems capable of performing multiple beneficial tasks, and (2) minimizing random fluctuations in these tasks. In classical devices, eliminating random fluctuations requires high entropy generation as dictated by thermodynamic uncertainty principles. Recent research indicates that ensembles have distinct benefits, particularly in uncertainty assessment and adaptability to dataset changes. This study demonstrates the limitations of these benefits, revealing that a single larger model can achieve similar outcomes. Firstly, ensemble diversity has no substantial effect on assessing uncertainty in out-of-distribution data; it mainly correlates with the improvement seen in a larger model. Secondly, an ensemble's ability to adapt to distribution changes is largely determined by the type of models used and the parameters adjusted, rather than being a sole consequence of the ensemble structure. While ensemble methods provide advantages in predictive accuracy, uncertainty assessment, and adaptability, this research shows that these benefits can be replicated by employing a single larger model, making the ensemble method redundant in these aspects. However, the ensemble method remains superior in facilitating collaborative learning and handling task diversity. Consequently, this research suggests that the superiority of ensembles over single models is more due to the characteristics of the models being compared, rather than any inherent advantage inherent to the ensemble method. Moreover, the study proposes a set of conditions that, when met, enable a single larger model to match the performance of an ensemble, potentially leading to the development of algorithms that identify such situations. Finally, the research highlights potential areas for further exploration in understanding the behavior of complex models. The study's code is available on GitHub

This study examines how GAN training is affected by high-frequency components.
During the typical GAN training process, significant high-frequency differences compel the discriminator to excessively focus on high-frequency features.
This issue restricts the generator from capturing the low-frequency features critical to capturing the image content.
We present two straightforward yet effective techniques to mitigate these adverse effects:
High-Frequency Confusion (HFC) and High-Frequency Filter (HFF).
These techniques are versatile and can be applied to various GAN architectures at a low computational cost.
The superior performance of our techniques is confirmed on multiple performance metrics, architectures, and datasets.
Specifically, the HFF approach leads to notable enhancements of 42.5%, 30.2%, and 69.3% in the FID metric for SNGAN, SSGAN, and InfoMAXGAN respectively when generating high-quality images on CelebA. has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. This speedup is all the more noteworthy since the Monte Carlo method itself already runs quickly. Moreover, we found that the Monte Carlo method overestimates the p-value only slightly, while being much slower than the exact algorithm. In contrast, we identified a situation in which the Monte Carlo method produced a misleadingly low p-value that was less than 0.1, when in fact the exact p-value was greater than 0.99. These findings suggest that using the exact algorithm can provide a safe and timely verification of statistical significance without prolonging operations. This conclusion holds true even when using the exact algorithm on larger datasets. In particular, we noted that the time it takes to compute the exact p-value is directly proportional to the square root of the sample size. As a result, we see the potential for our exact algorithm to enhance the statistical analysis of larger NLP systems in the future.

Although it has been extended to cover recursive data structures on the heap, gradual verification has a significant drawback - users do not reap the benefit of decreased dynamic checks as specifications improve, and all properties continue to be dynamically validated regardless of any static guarantees. dynamics of a two-mode nonlinear optical system is explored. Originating from a difference-frequency generation process, this system exhibits unique properties such as quantum correlations and entanglement. Our research shows that a strongly chirped pulse can reverse the direction of entanglement formation, and that in certain situations, it can generate a maximally entangled state from an initially separable one. Furthermore, we observe that a pulse's frequency agility aids this process, and that these effects can be observed even in systems lacking phase matching. Our findings offer novel strategies for creating entangled states via nonlinear interactions. The utility of our approach is confirmed by comparing two implementations, one involving chirped sideband generation and the other simulated through the fourth-wave mixing of solitons. The demonstrated ability to control entanglement formation through changes in pulse chirping presents a valuable technique for creating correlated photon states. The intricate interplay of classical and quantum properties underlying nonlinear optical systems is central to this research. The techniques outlined can be applied across a range of nonlinear transformations to generate tailored photon states. The underlying physics of these systems, governed by the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, holds significant practical value. The methods presented here may also facilitate the efficient creation of entangled states in systems involving phonons. The generality of our approach suggests that these techniques can be adapted and scaled up for use in quantum information applications. The critical factor is the degree of photon pair generation, which must be optimized to achieve maximal entanglement.

This paper showcases an advanced adaptive experimentation technique, known as the double spiral design, which has previously only been used in pharmaceutical trials but can be highly effective in educational research. Various elements influence a person's job selection, such as compatibility with the work environment, financial compensation, and degree of autonomy allowed.  A job candidate successfully fulfills their occupation by minimising the discrepancy between the skills required for the job and their own proficiency.  Reducing this gap between skills leads to better job compatibility.  In this research paper, we suggest creating a dynamic database of jobs and skills, which takes into account changing employment trends by combining existing classification systems with data on job listings.  This skills hierarchy is then used to calculate each candidate's remaining skills to fill, based on the skills demanded by remaining job openings.  Unlike existing approaches that focus on matching skills one by one or predicting skill preferences based on the candidate's past experiences, our proposed method allows for real-time analysis of the connection between a candidate's skills and job requirements.  Furthermore, we present several algorithms designed to reduce the skills gap between jobs and candidates, including ones that consider the candidate's past experiences and those that use skill embeddings based on the candidate's availability.  These algorithms are shown to improve job compatibility for candidates across various scenarios.  Additionally, the value of improving job compatibility using the proposed database and algorithmic contributions is quantified by measuring the candidate's remaining skills to fill. We introduce a kernel-based approach to generating data-driven models for high-dimensional, nonlinear systems. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse. This relationship is particularly evident within the subpopulation of white dwarf progenitors that undergo this transformation to become neutron star progenitors, ultimately giving rise to millisecond pulsars. Furthermore, our statistical analysis reveals a notable lower limit on the typical duration of the accretion phase relative to the duration of the pre-white dwarf stage ($\tau_{\rm acc} \gtrsim 10^{8.5}$ years), along with a upper limit on the typical duration of the pre-white dwarf stage relative to the duration of the accretion phase ($\tau_{\rm WD} \lesssim 10^{10.5}$ years). Additionally, our analysis yields a narrow range of possible typical masses for neutron stars, generally centered around 1.35 solar masses. The constraints provided by our analysis for the mass range of neutron stars smooth over discrepancies between different individual measurement methods. This research contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the final stages of stellar evolution

omechanical resonators, engineered to have ultra-low dissipation, have numerous applications, including quantum transduction and high-sensitivity sensing techniques. Traditionally, improving their performance, measured by their Qf product (quality factor times frequency), relied heavily on intuition and insight-based engineering approaches. These methods were often inefficient and overlooked the potential of alternative designs. This study, however, employs a cutting-edge computer-aided design technique known as topology optimization to develop ultra-efficient nanomechanical resonators. By utilizing this innovative approach, ultra-coherent resonators were created with exceptional Qf products, exhibiting coherent oscillations at room temperature. Furthermore, refinements to the underlying mechanical models may lead to even better performance. This new design paradigm can also be applied to other advanced resonators, unlocking novel technological applications and paving the way for pioneering research in fundamental physics and high-sensitivity sensing at room temperature. Additionally, the study provides a new theoretical framework for room-temperature resonators that could lead to a new class of nanomechanical devices. Finally, the research demonstrates a novel method for accurately evaluating the performance of nanomechanical resonators and other complex devices, known as the "volume penalty." This technique determines the optimal size of devices based on their material properties, revealing new insights into the underlying physics of nanomechanics and opening doors to developing highly optimized resonators and other micro- and nanomechanical devices.

requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, designed to improve performance in multi-goal scenarios by selectively retaining both short-term and long-term memories.
The short-term memory in MemoNav stores dynamic agent topological maps, updated as navigation progresses. To augment this memory, a graph attention module aggregates past short-term memories to generate a long-term memory.
A forgetting module using a Transformer decoder retains only the informative fraction of the short-term memory, ensuring that both the updated short-term memory and the accumulated long-term memory are integrated into the working memory, guiding action generation.
Experimental evaluations of MemoNav on a new dataset demonstrate significantly better performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches using a fraction of the navigation history, with reduced instances of deadlock situations. This research demonstrates that the action change resulting from trapping can be theoretically determined regardless of the rate of dynamic variation by combining perturbative and non-adiabatic methods. Tychonoff space can be given several equivalent topological structures by viewing them as either a union of groups of homeomorphisms with the same support size or as a subset of the group of homeomorphisms of its compactified space. A space has the CSHP if these two definitions yield the same topological space, which is the main topic of the paper's methods to prove that product spaces of specific spaces with CSHP possess CSHP. The paper also establishes that product spaces of spaces with finite CSHP are exactly those that can be broken down into a product of spaces where each factor either has finite CSHP or is compact. It is proven that the CSHP property is not completely eliminated when taking the topological sum of spaces with CSHP. The paper goes on to provide equivalent conditions for the CSHP property in terms of maps with compact support that are point-faithful and local homeomorphisms, which are then used to demonstrate that product spaces of spaces with finite CSHP are those that can be broken down into a product of spaces where each factor either has finite CSHP or is compact. Furthermore, the paper provides necessary and sufficient conditions for the CSHP property in terms of maps with compact support that are point-faithful and local homeomorphisms. Finally, the paper shows that the CSHP property is preserved under continuous maps to spaces with CSHP and that it is not completely eliminated when taking the topological sum of spaces with CSHP

The growth function of any algebra with a finite number of generators, which is also infinite in size, will naturally follow an increasing and submultiplicative pattern.
The extent to which the previously-mentioned growth function criteria (increasing and submultiplicative) act as a complete set of necessary conditions was a subject posed and explored by numerous authors, prompting a great deal of research in this area.

Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction are strategic, in contrast to a credible second-price auction where many bids are claimed to be based on a private valuation process. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species compete for resources, and we introduce a metric that determines sensitivity variations among species in response to changes in their environment. The introduction of this metric allows us to pinpoint precise thresholds that indicate a likelihood for population instability based on specific environmental conditions. The consequences of crossing these threshold values include significant population shifts, changes in consumption patterns, and alterations in resource availability. The findings obtained through numerical analysis match the theoretical predictions derived from the model's equilibrium analysis, and they reveal that population behavior is highly dependent on the relative sensitivities of the two species. The presence of critical tipping points, limited by the intersection points of the species' sensitivity curves, indicates potential regime shifts. The findings of this study demonstrate that early warning indicators for population instability appear in two phases, primarily in dynamics related to consumption patterns, and they persist for a prolonged period, largely influenced by the resource availability dynamics. The onset of these warning signals closely correlates with critical population ratios, and in some cases, with consumption patterns. The duration and timing of these warning indicators, however, are significantly influenced by the species' sensitivity ratio and availability dynamics. The model's framework can be applied to various ecosystem models that feature species with distinct sensitivity levels and shared resources. This study provides new insights into the mechanisms that contribute to population shifts, and it offers potential strategies for preventing regime shifts in ecological systems

(VQA) for visually-rich documents aims to bridge Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision by generating natural language responses to queries posed against complex document formats containing semi-structured tables and unstructured text. We introduce the TAT-DQA dataset, a comprehensive resource of 3,067 document pages sourced from authentic financial reports, paired with 16,558 question-answer sets. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques, especially when few labeled data are available. Moreover, the system's capability to learn a common feature that can be shared across different categories of input data significantly improves the performance, especially when little category information is available. Furthermore, the system's robustness is validated through various experiments including adversarial attacks and shows a significant improvement in performance when trained under attack scenarios.

This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if and only if certain conditions are met concerning their exponential sums. We take a step further by developing a more complex set of ring identities for constructing higher-dimensional arrays and use it to generate numerous quadruples of GCA in three-dimensional space. This research provides a detailed analysis of recent findings concerning multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and proposes a set of ring identities for their construction. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Unfortunately, accurately predicting the duration a program may run, or even whether it will stop, is generally infeasible.
As a result, modern analysis tools typically focus on specific operations and rely on several simplifying assumptions.
Precisely identifying these constraints and critical program regions generally necessitates access to source code, specialized tools, and domain expertise.
Modifying even a single instruction often forces a repeat of this complex process, which becomes extremely time-consuming during iterative code development for performance-critical software.
We introduce MCAD, a new lightweight framework for analyzing the effects of code modifications at the microarchitectural level in binary programs, providing fast and accurate estimates of throughput changes.
MCAD employs a combination of whole-program emulation and instruction-level analysis, facilitated by common tools, allowing developers to identify critical execution paths rapidly with minimal overhead.
To our knowledge, MCAD uniquely addresses the challenge of rapid turnaround times for throughput estimation by orders of magnitude, outperforming current best tools.
A detailed assessment reveals MCAD to effectively scale for large programs with millions of instructions like FFmpeg and Clang, yielding < 3% average error in throughput estimation compared to hardware measurements. 
Our case studies also demonstrate MCAD to provide insightful latency insights not previously attainable with existing tools. 
In particular, MCAD facilitates rapid analysis of code modifications for the performance-critical kernel sched_scpi, guiding developer decisions

In biology, information that's passed on is tricky to spot in pre-biotic systems described through chemical and physical principles. This text delves into one description using continuous-time Markov processes, focusing on how heritable information endures in large groups of dynamical systems, even with the constant fluctuation of their individual states. In these sets of systems, few relax at an exceptionally slow rate to their stationary distribution over extended periods. Those selected for their persistence also exhibit mesoscopic organization, facilitating the long-time description of their dynamics with high precision. This stable pattern's gradual decline is fueled by dissipative currents, which are generated by the existing thermodynamic gradients in their surroundings. We show how the production rate of entropy within a system determines an upper limit on its long-lived patterns. We then analyze the likelihood of persistence among numerous systems of various sizes, demonstrating that continuous and localized constraints significantly affect this likelihood and its dependency on system scale. Lastly, we outline a practical method for quantifying heritable information, utilizing universal compression algorithms, which we then demonstrate on magnetically-driven colloidal rollers and explore the implications of this approach for studying life's origins. This integrated theoretical framework, spanning physical and biological principles, provides a new understanding of life's requirements and the diverse forms they take. A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.

a highly successful technique called self-supervised learning (SSL), requiring zero manual annotations. A range of innovative methods have been developed in an attempt to surpass supervised alternatives. A significant challenge in SSL lies in ensuring that its approaches remain robust across different environments. This paper marks a first in acknowledging that SSL has inherent limitations arising from its reliance on a single guiding principle. To overcome these limitations, we have leveraged uncertainty representation to create a more robust and universally applicable hierarchical training protocol that is compatible with any existing SSL model. This improved approach is based on a fundamental concept called the information bottleneck principle and decomposes the feature learning process into two distinct training phases with separate supervision mechanisms. This dual-supervision strategy encompasses two pivotal steps: 1) a self-supervision phase that maximizes the reduction of input entropy, followed by 2) a pseudo-supervision phase that incorporates a robust uncertainty estimation technique to rectify errors that occurred during the first phase and pin down ambiguous cases. This two-phase training protocol has been universally applied to three distinct SSL methods and three popular metric learning benchmarks in order to conduct a comprehensive evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed protocol successfully enhances the cross-domain robustness of current state-of-the-art SSL models, further showcasing its versatility using three different benchmark sets. This is the first time that a robust hierarchical training protocol has been implemented for SSL models. A publicly accessible implementation of our approach is available at https://github.com/djhurst/dtt_uncertainty_based_self_sup

Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, the article goes on to address an additional problem, one not originally posed by Menger, in order to characterize those metric spaces with the property of betweenness that can be embedded into the structure of Euclidean spaces. This work also results in the identification of two novel, distinct types of metric spaces with the property of betweenness. Lastly, the relationships between the concepts of geodesics, isometry, and betweenness in metric spaces are explored. Specifically, the article shows that the embedding map employed in the solutions to Menger's problems preserves geodesics and isometry, but not necessarily the concept of betweenness. Conversely, the article does prove that the space of betweenness in metric spaces is preserved by the projection map. Finally, the article closes with a discussion of potential research avenues. Numerical simulations employing Particle in Cell (PIC) codes are a viable option to accomplish this task. By discretizing the plasma and defining electromagnetic fields on a grid, PIC codes can simulate the complex interactions involved in this phenomenon. Through our research, we explore how these adversarial examples behave internally within trained neural networks by examining their activation patterns in the hidden layers. Our study, focusing on different adversarial examples with varying characteristics, reveals unique features among them as they approach class-specific boundaries within these internal representations. To facilitate comparison, we developed two approaches that can measure proximity to these boundaries, unaffected by the shifting dimensions of the neural network. These measures then correlate with the confidence the network has in its predictions, as well as with human judgments on the similarity of the adversarial examples to their respective bases. These connections suggest that internal network representations capture relevant aspects of the manipulated features, allowing the network to internally evaluate the similarity of the examples to their bases. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the adversarial examples we studied mimic many aspects of their benign counterparts in their internal representations but diverge in their predicted classes. Our research provides a new insight into the internal workings of the adversarial phenomenon, shedding light on the nature of the manipulated features and their relation to the network's predictions. Our study also sets the stage for future investigations of other types of manipulated inputs and their behavior within neural networks. Pseudo-ensemble methods like dropout have been a staple in deep learning, but existing techniques have a significant drawback for uncertainty quantification - they require extensive computational resources. This paper presents the Uncertify framework, a comprehensive tool that surpasses state-of-the-art pseudo-ensemble methods by achieving accurate uncertainty quantification without compromising generalization. Uncertify's novel approach lies in utilizing various deep learning techniques to mimic primary model components, producing an approximate pseudo-ensemble with minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that Uncertify significantly enhances uncertainty estimation while promoting robust generalization, outperforming current methods. Existing methods for adjusting a robot's trajectory or impedance have focused on specific uncertainties, such as detecting human intentions or uncertainty-based learning from demonstration. These approaches fall short in addressing multiple uncertainties that commonly occur in tasks. This study introduces a more comprehensive framework to improve adaptability - using model predictive control (MPC) to simultaneously plan a robot's trajectory and impedance. This MPC method can address various uncertainties, prioritize safety constraints, and be applied efficiently across tasks. Key sources of uncertainty considered include variable contact constraints, shifting human goals, or unforeseen disturbances. To develop an adaptable task model, Gaussian Processes are used to analyze a few demonstrations (up to three). This model then informs an MPC problem to optimize the robot's trajectory and impedance, taking multiple uncertainties into consideration, particularly frequent uncertainties like variable contact constraints. This MPC formulation can be computed in real-time, allowing it to be applied in real-world scenarios, as seen in an experiment using a bimanual collaboration scenario. This technique has been successfully tested across multiple tasks including a collaborative assembly, a waste collection task, and a collaborative lifting scenario, indicating its potential to handle complex multi-faceted uncertainties to improve adaptability. This research is valuable to users seeking to handle various uncertainties in tasks to improve adaptability. We introduce a novel camera model validation method, evaluating performance through a perception algorithm and the context of measurement, distinct from traditional methods which typically rely on pixel or feature matching between synthetic and real images. As paired image acquisition is often impractical due to cost and constraints, our approach leverages datasets not requiring paired imagery, comparing real and simulated data through statistical analysis of subsets with similar content. Deep learning approaches are well-suited to addressing the intricate nature of image captioning challenges. This survey aims to provide an in-depth examination of deep learning-based image captioning methods, analyzing their underpinnings, successes, and shortcomings, as well as reviewing widely-used datasets and evaluation criteria. Following an overview of deep learning-based image captioning, this survey examines multiple aspects, including the identification of visual elements, their characteristics, relationships, and text generation. Several prominent methods and their variants are discussed, along with the implications of using pre-trained models and the potential for further improvement through data augmentation. The current state of the field is assessed, and potential future research directions are explored, including the integration of external knowledge and more sophisticated modeling of visual element interactions. The survey summarizes the progress made in the field by citing relevant studies and provides extensive references for further study. It primarily focuses on deep learning-based image captioning, known as visual captioning, distinguishing it from other related tasks such as zero-shot captioning, cross-lingual captioning, and generative captioning. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive insight into the development of deep learning-based image captioning, enabling readers to understand the subject and navigate the recent literature. It is particularly beneficial for graduate students and researchers new to the field, as well as those considering related applications, such as visual question answering

The core challenge lies in determining the optimal time to shift from one operational mode to another, which often requires resolving conflicting information and can be contentious. To address this, we formally establish the concept of operational modes for a system and derive a set of abstract data types for evaluating and transitioning between these modes. Specifically, we employ simplicial complexes, both in theory and in practice, to represent the connections between modes, which we illustrate with a detailed case study of a wastewater treatment system. We also provide an online tool allowing users to navigate and visualise the simplicial complex representing mode transitions. To resolve the complex calculations involved in transitioning between modes, we employ quantum linear programming, which offers significantly faster solutions than traditional methods. We provide an online implementation of our mode-based design approach in the Coq proof assistant, which we leverage to derive mode transitions and perform analysis based on a system model, utilizing the fundamental concepts of operational modes we have established. We further provide a practical algorithm for a system's operation, which we detail using the example of a wastewater treatment plant. We provide an online interface for interacting with the modes of a system and performing calculations, which we utilize to derive decision and control algorithms for a system, which we demonstrate while navigating a crisis. We discuss the potential future applications of our work, which involves utilizing topological data analysis to inform operational mode design.

This paper focuses on r-truncated degenerate Stirling numbers of the second kind, 
which revert to standard degenerate Stirling numbers for r=1. It examines their 
mathematical expressions, notable properties, and related identities within a broader 
context of degenerate special numbers and polynomials. 
The r-truncated degenerate Stirling numbers of the second kind can be expressed as the 
degenerate Bell numbers divided by (r+1), with additional factors involving binomial 
coefficients. This expression reveals a connection to the truncated degenerate Bell 
numbers themselves. Further analysis reveals that multiple properties held by standard 
Stirling numbers of the second kind are preserved for their r-truncated degenerate 
counterparts. Additionally, we derive an identity related to a degenerate version of 
Euler's partition formula, which is itself a consequence of a broader formula for degenerate 
polynomials. This finding aligns with similar outcomes seen in the study of special 
numbers and polynomials. 
The focus on r-truncated degenerate Stirling numbers of the second kind serves as a 
starting point to explore similar objects, such as r-truncated degenerate Stirling 
numbers of the first kind, as well as other related special numbers and polynomials. 
This presents opportunities to generalize results seen in the study of degenerate numbers

Although magnetic field models are more detailed, they often result in equilibrium configurations that are too simplistic to effectively represent the complex nature of stellar formation. In contrast, non-ideal magnetic field models that incorporate Hall and Ohm's laws into the ideal magnetohydrodynamics framework offer a more suitable approach to understanding the process. Through three distinct models of global simulations, this study investigates the impact of ambient conditions on the embryonic star's formation, focusing on a scenario with internal and external instabilities. A comparison of the models reveals a shift from turbulent convection to differential rotation and infall dynamics based on the ambient angular momentum ratio, but unlike ideal magnetohydrodynamics models, all non-ideal models exhibit disk fragmentation under specific conditions. As the ambient angular momentum ratio increases, disk fragmentation is replaced by infall dynamics in the non-ideal models, in contrast to the critical mass-to-specific angular momentum ratio greater than 10 in the ideal models. Furthermore, a sub-allocation of angular momentum within the disk leads to disk fragmentation in the models that incorporate the Hall effect, but not in the models without it. Despite differences in the accretion dynamics and disk structure, the models all result in similar stellar masses and disk masses, indicating that the global stellar and disk formation are robust to local ambient conditions and magnetic field influences

for object clustering have been noteworthy due to the enhanced clustering performance achieved through incorporating tactile data. Despite this progress, the persistent problem of missing data, resulting from data collection issues like occlusion and noise, remains a challenge to be overcome. The majority of current methods designed to handle partial data in multi-view clustering settings have not successfully addressed the inherent complexity of heterogeneous modalities. Applying these existing methods would only lead to further degradation of performance. In response to this, we introduce the Generative Partial Visual-Tactile Fused framework (GPVTF) for object clustering. The framework starts by separately extracting partial visual and tactile features from the respective datasets, followed by encoding these features in modality-specific spaces. A conditional cross-modal clustering GAN then generates one modality conditioned on the other, thereby compensating for missing samples and synchronizing visual and tactile data through adversarial learning. The encoders' corresponding modality-specific spaces are then refined through KL-divergence losses based on pseudo-labels. Thorough experiments conducted on three publicly accessible datasets reveal the effectiveness of our GPVTF approach over current state-of-the-art methods designed for partial visual-tactile fused object clustering. The source code for GPVTF can be found at the link: https://github.com/IndigoPurple/GPVTF.

Research on planets in these stars' habitable zones has focused primarily on the habitable zones at the center of the day-side where temperatures are mild, due to their synchronized rotation causing large differences between the day and night sides. This paper instead examines the possibility of habitable climates in areas where day meets night on planets in these zones, known as terminator regions, by employing a comprehensive climate model. According to this model, planets that lack sufficient water can maintain relatively mild temperatures near the terminator by having little energy being transferred through their atmosphere, resulting in scorching temperatures near the center of the day-side and freezing temperatures on the night-side. Conversely, planets rich in water show less significant day-night temperature differences due to increased heat transfer through their atmosphere, as more stellar radiation is absorbed. Nonetheless, this water abundance can also lead to water loss through surface condensation and atmospheric escape, which in turn reduces their habitable capacity, suggesting that even water-rich planets could transition to water-limited planets and possibly support terminator habitable climates. Ultimately, observations of planets in these zones will require novel approaches, as current methods fail to adequately account for their synchronized rotation and temperature differences between the day and night sides. This paper suggests using color and spectral type information to identify these planets, as they tend to have cooler day-side temperatures and thus different colors compared to central habitable zone planets with similar properties. The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the type and extent of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct damage patterns in both artificial and real-world tests.
The results revealed the efficacy of this hybrid approach in enhancing reconstruction accuracy and extracting vital information about damage area, orientation, and thickness in multiple laminated composites subjected to various loads. 
The proposed method demonstrated a high degree of stability and precision, with dimensions calculated at 0.35% error for impact tests and 1.5% error for wedge fatigue.
The success of this approach was confirmed by its superior performance on 14 different types of CFRP laminates, showcasing its potential for practical application in the future. 
The method's reliability and robustness were further validated by its correct reconstruction of damage in two practical examples, including a thick, 10-layer composite and a helicopter blade.

The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations. considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: 

1. Identifying negated statements within passages.
2. Determining the scope of negation.
3. Assessing the truth of statements that were not directly negated but were present in the passage.

Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging questions, along with an accompanying benchmark of systems, and we present several innovative, negation-aware models. Although these models performed well on existing benchmarks of NLP systems, they struggled with CONDAKA, particularly when it came to determining the scope of negation. This prompted researchers to re-examine the role of attention and positional information in the interpretation of negation, leading to the development of several cutting-edge, negation-aware models. To further enhance the practical applications of NLP, we encourage the broader research community to utilize CONDAQA, with the goal of developing models capable of effectively processing negation. This dataset is available at https://condaqa.org/.

Successfully implemented, these attacks can substantially compromise the reliability of machine learning models and cause significant financial losses, all while remaining nearly undetectable. As research into backdoor attacks continues to evolve, many approaches remain restricted to specific datasets, rendering them less effective against more complex datasets, such as those involving high-dimensional image data. In contrast, previous methods focused on triggering backdoors through ubiquitous inputs have limitations, including increased detectability and a higher likelihood of being replaced by more sophisticated techniques. To address these issues, we introduce the Data Marking backdoor attack, which overcomes the existing challenges and effectively works on various datasets, including those derived from network traffic. This oversight limits our understanding of the spontaneous, collective processes aiming to optimize or restore synchronized systems, such as cardiac cell communication. We introduce a novel 'grass-roots' approach to synchronization, where local improvements in smaller components collectively optimize the entire system. Using cardiac tissue and power grid models, we demonstrate that systems optimized through this grass-roots mechanism can be just as efficient as those globally optimized but are also resilient to targeted attacks and system disruptions. These findings validate the need for further investigation into local mechanisms that can facilitate self-optimization in complex systems. The synchronization of such systems can be viewed as a manifestation of the 'emergence' principle, where organized patterns and behaviors arise from the collective interaction of basic, locally-optimized components. Our work opens doors for exploring self-optimization strategies at the cardiac and power grid levels, while contributing to a broader understanding of synchronization in complex systems. The concepts presented can also inform the design of efficient, fault-tolerant networks through the implementation of grass-roots synchronization. The optimization theory can now be applied to systems that do not require global information, illustrating the power of local mechanisms in synchrony.

Traditional motion planning techniques based on heuristics like frontier-based methods excel in environments where the layout is unknown. Nevertheless, these methods may fall short when statistical data about the environment's design is readily available, leading to less optimal outcomes and extended computation times. In this study, we present two solutions to mitigate these limitations. The first approach leverages deep reinforcement learning to train a motion planning system. The second involves utilizing a pre-trained deep neural network that can forecast environmental layouts. Both techniques capitalize on learned environmental patterns to refine decision-making and operate within a constant computational framework. The integration of these methods results in a substantial decrease of up to 4 times in the time required to map out a space when compared to heuristic-based motion planning. The trained models also demonstrate a notable enhancement in overall performance, amounting to a 20% increase in success rates and a 30% reduction in completion times when compared to their heuristic-based counterparts. The developed framework is thoroughly evaluated across three diverse indoor environments, showcasing its robustness and consistency across all tested scenarios. US banks involves regulatory stress tests using proprietary models to evaluate the performance of individual banks in shared stress scenarios.  The uniform application of these models to diverse institutions has been a topic of contention, as banks claim certain models are ill-suited to their respective business models.  Our investigation stems from this debate: How can the collective output of individualized models be fairly combined into a single framework?  The method of pooling data across institutions treats all banks equally, yet it is vulnerable to two limitations - it may misrepresent the effects of legitimate portfolio factors and it relies on an implicit inference of a bank's identity based on information.  To address these concerns, we examine different fairness concepts in regression analysis, balancing both predictive accuracy and fair treatment, and we apply our approach to estimate stress test results.  Our results show that using a weighted average of individualized model outputs with weights based on observable bank characteristics can closely mimic the stress test methodology's pooling method, while also ensuring fairness.  The weight estimates suggest that certain bank characteristics - such as total assets and return on equity - play a significant role in determining model pooling weights.  However, when considering the stress test scenarios in question, our findings indicate that the output of the individualized models is most influenced by total assets, followed by earnings, and then credit quality.  The weight estimates also hold value outside of stress testing contexts within banking regulations, as they relate to aspects of a bank's overall business model and can provide insight into systemic risks.

jets are closely linked to the process of mass accretion and provide valuable insights into the development of star formation. To gain a deeper understanding of these complex processes, scientists are studying the variability in mass-ejection events during the early stages of star formation. Researchers have observed CO and SO emission from the NOEMA telescope directed at the intermediate-mass star-forming system Cep E. Their observations reveal a high-velocity jet composed of knots that originate near the star, surrounded by a slower-moving gas layer. As this gas moves away from the star, its velocity and diameter increase, causing the jet to collapse and form slower-moving lobes. Further analysis indicates that the lobe structure in CO and C$^{18}$O emission corresponds to regions where the jet interacts with a surrounding disc gas layer. In contrast, SO emission is primarily confined to the faster-moving jet core, suggesting that the slower-moving gas layer is largely suppressed in this region. As the jet breaks through the disc, it creates cylindrical shapes in gas and dust, observed here for the first time in the CO and continuum emission. Models of jet-circumstellar disc interactions need to be revised to include a disc that is both less massive and less dense in the vicinity of the jet. In addition, it appears that mass accretion onto the star may be temporarily slowed or accelerated in response to changes in disc structure and dynamics. To gain further insights into these complex processes, scientists are planning additional observations with the NOEMA telescope

A new, optimized hardware accelerator for Deep Forest models is proposed, which is the first of its kind to implement Deep Forest on a Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA). This solution involves developing a specialized node computing unit to accelerate processing and an efficient data handling approach to balance computational load during classification tasks. Furthermore, a customized storage scheme is designed to enhance hardware efficiency and reduce energy consumption. Experimental results indicate that the new accelerator yields a substantial 40 times increase in processing speed over a high-performance 40-core CPU. Additionally, the area required for the Deep Forest accelerator is only a fraction (around 1/13) of the corresponding area for a neural network accelerator on the same FPGA. This results in the world's first Deep Forest model to be implemented on a large scale, comprising 7 layers with 716822 nodes, which is capable of achieving 171.8 seconds of latency with an impressive 98.13% accuracy in the data. This marks the first time a state-of-the-art Deep Forest model has been implemented on an FPGA. When compared to a high-performance 40-core CPU, the new Deep Forest model exhibits superior performance in various forecasting tasks, including the M4 competition series and additional evaluation datasets, which it outperforms by a significant margin

The intricacy of adversarial examples presents a major challenge in detailing their phenomenon, thus many studies simplify this complex issue, proposing theoretical models and testing them to predict specific aspects of adversarial examples. These research studies explore multiple facets of adversarial examples but have yet to develop a comprehensive understanding through geometric and analytical modeling. This research presents a formal framework to analyze and study the phenomenon in machine learning, employing complex analysis and holomorphicity to develop a reliable learning approach for artificial neural networks, enabling an easy shift between the geometric and analytical views of the phenomenon and its connection to harmonic functions.
