employed in the cognitive sciences to perform null hypothesis testing, comparing a null hypothesis that a given effect equals zero against an alternative hypothesis stating the effect's existence and difference from zero. However, despite the availability of software for Bayes factor null hypothesis testing, accurately specifying the data and model can often be a challenge. Various researchers recommend aggregating data by subject and performing Bayes factor analyses on these aggregated datasets within a Bayesian framework. Yet, we use simulation-based model calibration to demonstrate that null hypothesis testing from aggregated data can result in biased Bayes factors, due in part to the violation of sphericity assumptions resulting from random slope variance differences. Consequently, Bayes factors are found to be overly conservative for smaller variance contrasts and excessively liberal for larger variance contrasts. Moreover, we find Bayes factors for subject-aggregated data to be biased when ignoring random item variance present in the data, though yielding overly liberal results in such scenarios. To combat these issues, we also perform corresponding frequentist analyses (type I and II error rates) highlighting the existence and common recognition of similar problems using traditional tools. To circumvent these challenges, we suggest running Bayesian linear mixed-effects models on unaggregated data, individual trial-level, while accounting for the full complexity of the random effects structure. In bioinformatics, this is useful for connecting patient data across different medical databases but also raises confidentiality concerns. To address these concerns, a homomorphic encryption protocol known as HEA2 has been implemented, allowing for the comparison of sensitive information while preserving privacy. In addition, an efficient and previously unpublished method has been developed to reduce comparison processing time by breaking down the comparison process into smaller steps and only combining the results if those steps yield matching sub-string values. In terms of performance, the results show that the use of a hard drive as an additional layer of encryption significantly enhances security at only a minor cost in terms of increased processing time. This is achieved through the management of a series of partial results accumulated throughout the database linking process and reveals a direct relationship between database size and the associated processing time. We introduce a novel approach that significantly diverges from standard methods for solving deterministic partial differential equations. Our work has far-reaching applications for stochastic hydrodynamic equations as well as their deterministic counterparts. Furthermore, we develop a random version of the maximum principle for 3D Burgers equations, which is crucial for exploring the behavior of stochastic 3D Burgers equations. One major challenge in this field is obtaining moment estimates for nonlinear stochastic equations, as they are pivotal in understanding probabilistic characteristics and long-term behavior of stochastic systems. Fortunately, our random maximum principle facilitates the derivation of significant moment estimates for 3D stochastic Burgers equations, thus providing a strong foundation for future research on these systems. Additionally, our study offers a new perspective on the dissipative mechanism in turbulent flows, suggesting that large-scale multiplicative noise can lead to enhanced dissipation even in the absence of a quadratic nonlinearity. This concept is particularly noteworthy, as it is generally believed that linear and quartic interactions are the most efficacious for energy dissipation. Our work not only provides a new approach to low-regularity stochastic equations but also offers a fresh insight into the behavior of energy dissipation in turbulent flows and their stochastic counterparts. To confirm our hypotheses, we conduct numerical simulations that verify our theoretical findings on the dissipative properties of 3D stochastic Burgers equations. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to reach its full size, whereas in the south, it formed almost immediately in the spring. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strong temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude, which served as the boundary that distinguishes it from the surrounding atmosphere. The vortex in the south, on the other hand, had a more irregular shape and lacked a defined boundary until the last week of the summer, even though it was surrounded by a temperature gradient at 85 degrees latitude. The formation of these polar vortices is closely linked to the influence of the planet's rotation and the uneven distribution of ultraviolet radiation, which varies greatly between the two hemispheres due to the tilt of the Saturnian system. The vortex in the north was found to be composed of relatively warm air, which was arranged in a specific pattern, which was not observed in the warmer and larger vortex in the south.

The P / Poly class has been pivotal in historical attempts to address the equivalence between solution and verification - essentially, the P vs NP conundrum. Due to circuits' potentially simpler non-uniform computational nature (with program size allowed to adapt to input size), they may be more tractable than Turing Machines, but it is notoriously difficult to derive lower bounds for them. This report examines key results from Hastad, Sipser, and Razborov, showcasing a complex interplay between circuit complexity and foundational concepts of modern complexity theory, notably the crucial role of Hastad's Switching Lemma. Despite the challenges of circuit complexity, investigating lower bounds has become a central focus in understanding P / Poly and, by extension, the core P vs NP dilemma. Circuit complexity has significant implications for understanding verification processes, making it a crucial area of study in computer science. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. This approach provides a new, highly sensitive method for determining local magnetic fields, opening up further research applications in metrology, particularly in measuring superconductor parameters. 

A crucial aspect considered in this research involves differentiating between true Meissner effect, which represents the active expulsion of magnetic field through superconductivity, and the inverse Meissner effect, which represents the passive behavior of the superconductor boundary where external magnetic field strength is reduced. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators. These results include four distinct types: those with two modal operators and Dunn axioms, those with two modal operators, those with a primitive operator, and those with two binary operators. This is the first case where individual particles remain localized without being part of distinct eigenstates. Instead, their localization occurs within broad bands of many closely packed eigenstates, connected by terms that represent chiral interactions. These findings offer insights into the delicate balance between localization and the system's symmetry properties. We've also observed that these transitional states feature coherent transport characteristics, where particles move coherently over long distances, despite being localized. This is possible because the transitional states are characterized by a vast number of eigenstates that facilitate chiral tunneling. This type of tunneling allows for smooth and continuous transport patterns, even without being based on regular, uninterrupted wave patterns. We've seen this by looking at the system's entanglement entropy and the associated entanglement spectrum, which represents the way the system's quantum states are intertwined. The transitional states, resulting from the conflict between disorder and chiral symmetry, bring a new kind of localized matter that's distinct from the original localized and delocalized phases, offering a range of possibilities to explore coherent and localized transport in quantum systems. A crucial area of study within this field seeks to establish reliable predictors of gentrification and/or displacement, with a goal of developing proactive early warning systems. Since many relevant PBMs are difficult to solve analytically, researchers often rely on complex numerical methods, like high-order finite difference techniques, to produce reliable solutions, albeit at significant computational costs. we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency bursts at each close approach, but eventually, the surrounding disc becomes a sustained source of radiation, echoing patterns seen in stellar black hole systems, while the electromagnetic signals exhibit characteristics similar to those of pulsars. The intensity of these bursts diminishes over time as the white dwarf's mass decreases. Ultimately, the surrounding disc becomes the primary source of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, and our findings suggest that such systems may be responsible for a portion of the observed X-ray sources in the galaxy. The white dwarf's initial mass and distance from the black hole determine the duration and frequency of these bursts, and extensive numerical simulations are required to accurately analyze these systems. The potential for such systems to be detected by future gravitational wave observatories, including the James Webb Space Telescope, and the characterization of such systems through such detections, are discussed in the context of future research opportunities.

, a new type of hybrid network is suggested that blends rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  This hybrid network creates edges according to a mixture of these rules.  Specifically, when a new edge is added, it follows the preferential attachment rule with a certain probability and otherwise forms between two randomly selected nodes.  This approach leads to a distribution of node in- and out-degrees that has less extreme outliers compared to a purely preferential attachment network, thereby improving upon this traditional model.  Inference methods applicable to the new model are then explored and demonstrated with both artificially generated and actual network data, revealing the potential benefits of incorporating this flexible hybrid network into the study of real-world networks where such less extreme outcomes are typically observed.  In such cases, a more moderate distribution of node degrees may indicate the presence of underlying structural components or modules within the network.  Furthermore, the gradual transition from purely preferential attachment to this hybrid model, as influenced by the probability governing edge formation, offers a novel dimension for comparing different hybrid networks and interpreting the resulting differences in node degree distributions.  Ultimately, the simplicity and extensibility of this new model, combined with its capacity for accurately fitting network data and providing meaningful insights into network structure, are shown to be significant advantages.  Based on these results, the use of hybrid networks is suggested as a valuable strategy for the analysis of real-world network data, particularly when combined with methods for identifying and interpreting structural components or modules within such networks

Each agent in the swarm is represented by a position vector, $\boldsymbol{x}$, and a mass, $m$, which facilitates communication between them through the transfer of masses from high to low areas. Agents adjust their step size, $h=h(\boldsymbol{x},m)$, based on their relative mass: more massive agents move cautiously in the direction of the local gradient, whereas less massive ones use a backtracking protocol to take larger steps. As a result, the swarm dynamically separates into leaders, heavier agents, which are likely to reach local minima, and explorers, lighter agents, whose large steps may lead to the discovery of better positions for the swarm. Through local gradient adjustments, leaders become explorers, while explorers assume leadership if they successfully discover an improved position. Our analysis, supported by numerical simulations in various dimensions, demonstrates that the Swarm-Based Gradient Descent algorithm is a proficient global optimizer. Furthermore, we have adapted this algorithm to function in a distributed setting, where a leader agent, chosen at random, guides the swarm towards an optimized position without the need for communication between agents. Our results also show that the Distributed Swarm-Based Gradient Descent algorithm is an effective global optimizer. Our research centers on single layer networks where binary synapses are used to learn random patterns, a statistical problem where solutions are predominantly isolated and extremely difficult to locate algorithmically.

and their counterparts play a vital role in achieving goals and guiding optimization. However, these tools face practical and theoretical limitations when it comes to dealing with complex objectives that are difficult to combine or reduce to one another. Philosophers have discovered a number of impossibility theorems stemming from this challenge, indicating that there may be no effective way to define what it means for an outcome to be beneficial without disregarding fundamental human ethics. As this problem has significant implications for high-stakes systems like AI medical decision support and autonomous weapons, these systems should refrain from using objective functions in a strict mathematical sense.

One potential solution is to utilize uncertain objectives, such as partially ordered preferences or probability distributions over outcomes, instead of fixed objective functions. By exploring this alternative, it is possible to reinterpret previously established impossibility theorems as uncertainty theorems and derive lower bounds on the degree of uncertainty implied by these results. Ultimately, the relationship between objective uncertainty and unintended AI consequences remains a pressing question, prompting two key conjectures about the relationship between uncertainty and system malfunction. The indirect utilization of Reinforcement Learning methods for graph classification, given that datasets involve discrete graphs with labels, stands in contrast to traditional approaches that use direct gradient optimization. This work aims to explore the novel threat of data manipulation during training (Data Poisoning) targeting Graph Classification neural networks via Reinforcement Learning agents. Three distinct types of attackers have been researched, all seeking to skew a model to misclassify a specific label by manipulating a minority of training examples. The poisons are injected into the training set via a simulated Reinforcement Learning agent playing a game on a modified graph. The effectiveness of three existing attack strategies has been assessed against four Graph Classification models and three different training techniques. The experiments also investigated the effectiveness of a strategy based on the similarity of neighboring graphs. This study presents the first known instance of a successful Data Poisoning attack against a Graph Classification model, achieving a remarkable 50% success rate, which surpasses the baseline accuracy of the target model by 11.15%. The results also highlight the vulnerability of supervised graph learning to Reinforcement Learning-based Data Poisoning. Resource Allocation (ONRA) plays a vital role in service provisioning. As a sequential problem with uncertain outcomes, it presents a suitable case for tackling via Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, current RL solutions face significant challenges stemming from high sample complexity requirements. To navigate this hurdle, training RL agents in isolation is impractical due to a lack of knowledge about future service demands, while online learning in actual networks causes performance deterioration due to temporary sub-optimal policies during prolonged training periods. This degradation is particularly pronounced in non-stationary ONRA scenarios, where adapting to shifting service requirements is crucial. To circumvent this problem, a model-based resource allocation framework called RADAR is proposed, designed for ONRA applications with immediately known action rewards. By strategically balancing exploration of the state space in the background with real-time policy exploitation, leveraging synthetic data generated from the trained environment model, RADAR effectively boosts sample efficiency. Furthermore, empirical evidence collected from a diverse set of non-stationary ONRA scenarios highlights the substantial performance gains that RADAR achieves over both baseline RL models and the traditional, conventional approach to ONRA, illustrating the critical importance of environment modeling for optimizing the ONRA process. As such, the proposed model-based strategy can serve as a powerful tool to empower a broad spectrum of communication systems capable of instantiating tasks, thereby breaking the limitations imposed by the Law of Large Numbers in the realm of ONRA. However, addressing adversarial attacks during the base-data training phase presents unique challenges: given the diversity of CNN architectures and the vast number of possible classifiers, implementing robust defense mechanisms is a difficult task.  Our research introduces a data transformation method, combining a data standardizer with a Normalizing Flow, to neutralize adversarial attacks while maintaining feature data utility.  The proposed strategy is evaluated against several state-of-the-art defense mechanisms, yielding significant improvement in accuracy and feature utility for several CNN architectures, as well as providing a framework for quantifying utility preservation.  Specifically, our results show that the standardizer's utility preservation capability surpasses that of the comparative models by 93% and 34% respectively, and that the combined model achieves a 91% gain in accuracy while maintaining feature utility. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we introduce an efficient and straightforward H2ML method variation that simplifies the calculation of potential averages over arbitrary shapes. Our approach employs specific formulas combining the logarithmic averages of the near and far potentials to significantly reduce computational complexities, effectively from quadratic to linear dependencies on the number of grid cells. Through several numerical experiments, we demonstrate the speed and accuracy of our modified method variant compared to standard H2ML methods. Our findings show that this new implementation can solve complex, boundary-driven problems significantly faster than its conventional counterparts. Specifically, solving two-dimensional heat conduction equations and evaluating Newtonian potentials became nearly two and three times faster with our modified method. Furthermore, we observed a notable reduction in processing time of up to ten times for some scenarios. Our results indicate that this new implementation is not only more efficient but also more robust, as it effectively handled various difficult-to-solve cases, such as computing Green's function on complex shapes and solving boundary integral equations for irregular profiles, where conventional methods struggled or took extended time to compute.
